n: Paul begins his great chapter on the Resurrection by reminding the saints of the gospel he first preached — the gospel they accepted and on which they now stand.

f.w: the gospel which I preached unto you

n: This gospel saves them if they hold firmly to it — otherwise their belief would have been for nothing.
The heart of the message, which Paul himself received: Christ died for our sins, as the scriptures foretold.

f.g: Handed on — a term for passing down sacred tradition.

n: He was buried, and He rose again on the third day, just as scripture said.
Paul lists eyewitnesses: the risen Christ appeared to Peter, then to the Twelve.
He appeared to more than five hundred believers at once. Most were still alive and could be asked — a bold invitation to check the facts.

f.w: above five hundred brethren at once
f.g: This appearance is mentioned only here.

n: Then He appeared to James, the Lord’s brother, and to all the apostles.

f.g: Likely James the Lord’s brother, later a leader in Jerusalem.

n: Last of all He appeared to Paul, who calls himself like a child born at the wrong time — an apostle called unusually late.

f.g: An untimely birth — a vivid image of his sudden, irregular calling.

n: Paul sees himself as the least of the apostles, unworthy of the title, because he once persecuted the Church.

f.w: I persecuted the church of God

n: Yet God’s grace made him who he is, and it wasn’t wasted: Paul worked harder than anyone — though he credits God’s grace for it.

f.w: by the grace of God I am what I am

n: Whether Paul or the other apostles preached, the message was the same, and the Corinthians believed it.

f.g: The apostles taught a united witness.

n: If the risen Christ is preached, how can some Corinthians claim the dead don’t rise? Greek thinking often regarded the body as a prison to escape, not something to restore.
If there is no resurrection at all, then Christ Himself didn’t rise.

f.g: Paul follows the denial to its logical end.

n: And if Christ didn’t rise, all preaching and all faith are empty.
The apostles would then be lying about God, falsely testifying that He raised Christ.
Paul repeats the point: deny resurrection in general and you deny Christ’s.

f.g: The two stand or fall together.

n: If Christ isn’t raised, their faith is useless and they remain unforgiven. The Resurrection confirms that His Atonement worked.

f.w: ye are yet in your sins

n: And believers who died would simply be lost forever.
If our hope in Christ were only for this life, we would be the most pitiable people of all.
But Christ truly has risen! He is the firstfruits — the first portion of a harvest that guarantees the rest will follow.

f.g: The first sheaf of harvest offered to God, promising the full harvest.

n: Death came into the world through a man; resurrection comes through a man too.
Because of Adam, all die; because of Christ, all will be made alive again. The Resurrection is a universal gift.

f.w: in Christ shall all be made alive

n: There is an order: Christ first, then at His coming those who belong to Him, and others later.

f.w: every man in his own order

n: Then comes the end, when Christ, having conquered every opposing power, presents the kingdom to the Father.

f.w: delivered up the kingdom to God

n: Christ must reign until all enemies are under His feet, as the psalm foretold.

f.w: till he hath put all enemies under his feet

n: The final enemy Christ will destroy is death itself.
Quoting a psalm that God put all things under the Son’s feet, Paul notes that the Father who did this is of course not included.

f.w: he hath put all things under his feet

n: When all is subdued, the Son Himself will remain subject to the Father, so God will be all in all. Father and Son are distinct, perfectly united beings.

f.w: the Son also himself be subject

n: Paul points to a practice the Corinthians knew: baptism on behalf of the dead. It would make no sense if the dead never rise. Latter-day Saints perform this ordinance in temples today.
Why would the apostles risk danger every hour if there were no resurrection?
Paul swears by his pride in them: he faces death every day.
If he fought “beasts” at Ephesus — probably fierce human opponents — for no eternal purpose, he might as well live for pleasure. Paul quotes the hopeless motto of Isaiah’s day.

f.w: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die

n: Don’t be fooled: bad company ruins good character. Paul quotes a well-known Greek saying.

f.g: A line from the Greek poet Menander: bad company corrupts good morals.

n: Wake up to what is right and stop sinning. Some among them don’t truly know God — and that should shame them.
Paul anticipates a question: how are the dead raised? What kind of body will they have?
Look at a seed: it must be buried and “die” before new life springs up.
You plant a bare kernel, not the full plant that will grow.
God gives each seed the body He designed for it. The resurrected body is connected to the mortal one but far more glorious.

f.w: to every seed his own body

n: There are many kinds of bodies — humans, animals, fish, birds — each different.

f.w: All flesh is not the same flesh

n: There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies with different glories. The JST adds “bodies telestial,” matching the three degrees of glory revealed to Joseph Smith in D&C 76.
The sun, moon, and stars each shine with a different glory. Paul uses this to illustrate differing glories in the resurrection.

f.w: one star differeth from another star in glory

n: So with the resurrection: the body is buried subject to decay; it is raised never to decay again.

f.g: Buried in a body that decays.

n: Buried in humiliation and weakness, it is raised in glory and power.
It is buried a natural body and raised a spiritual body — still physical, but now governed by the spirit and immortal.

f.g: A body of flesh and bone quickened by spirit rather than blood.

n: Genesis says the first man, Adam, became a living soul. Christ, the “last Adam,” became a life-giving spirit who raises all.

f.w: The first man Adam was made a living soul

n: The natural body comes first, and the spiritual (resurrected) body comes afterward.
Adam was made from the earth; Christ is the Lord from heaven.
Mortals share Adam’s earthly nature; those who follow Christ will share His heavenly nature.
Just as we have borne Adam’s image, we will bear the image of the resurrected Christ.

f.w: bear the image of the heavenly

n: Mortal flesh and blood, in its corruptible state, can’t inherit God’s kingdom; it must be changed.

f.w: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God
f.g: Resurrected bodies are flesh and bone, not mortal flesh and blood.

n: Paul reveals a mystery: not everyone will die, but everyone will be transformed.
In an instant, at the final trumpet, the dead will rise imperishable and the living will be changed.
This decaying, mortal body must be clothed with incorruption and immortality.

f.w: this mortal must put on immortality

n: Then Isaiah’s prophecy will be fulfilled: death is swallowed up in victory.

f.w: Death is swallowed up in victory

n: Paul taunts death in Hosea’s words: Where is your sting? Where is your victory?

f.w: O death, where is thy sting?

n: Death’s sting is sin, and sin draws its power from the law, which exposes and condemns it.

f.w: the strength of sin is the law

n: But thanks be to God, who gives us victory over sin and death through Jesus Christ!
So stand firm and immovable, always giving yourselves fully to the Lord’s work, knowing that nothing you do for Him is wasted.
